subject: biology-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Diversity of organisms
bigPicture: No two organisms are identical, but they fall into species. Defining a species is harder than it sounds; chromosomes and genomes give new ways to compare organisms, and DNA barcoding can identify species from traces in the environment.

keyIdeas.cue: Why is variation a defining feature of life?
keyIdeas.answer: No two individuals are identical in all their traits. Patterns of variation are the basis for naming and classifying organisms.
The morphological concept: a species is a group of organisms sharing similar traits (appearance).

keyIdeas.cue: How does the binomial system work?
keyIdeas.answer: Two Latin names: Genus (capital letter) then species (lower case), e.g. Homo sapiens, written in italics (underlined if handwritten). Species in the same genus share similar traits.

keyIdeas.cue: What is the biological species concept and its problems?
keyIdeas.answer: A species is a group that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Problems: fossils and asexual organisms can't be tested; some species hybridise; it's impractical to test breeding in the wild. Other species concepts exist.

keyIdeas.cue: Why is it hard to tell populations from species?
keyIdeas.answer: Speciation (one species splitting into two or more) is usually gradual: isolated populations diverge bit by bit, so deciding when they become separate species is often arbitrary.
Yes, widely between species. Humans have 46, chimpanzees 48. Diploid cells have an even number because chromosomes come in pairs.

keyIdeas.cue: What is a karyogram and what does it show about human chromosome 2?
keyIdeas.answer: A karyogram arranges an individual's chromosomes in pairs by length, centromere position and banding pattern. Human chromosome 2 matches two separate ape chromosomes end to end, with remnants of telomeres in the middle and a second inactive centromere: evidence it formed by fusion of two chromosomes from a shared ancestor. This is a testable hypothesis.

keyIdeas.cue: How similar are genomes within a species?
keyIdeas.answer: The genome is all an organism's genetic information. Members of a species share most of it; small differences such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) give diversity.

keyIdeas.cue: How do eukaryote genomes differ between species?
keyIdeas.answer: In total size (amount of DNA) and in base sequence. Differences between species are much larger than within a species.
Not reliably: data from genome databases show some plants and amphibians have far bigger genomes than humans.

keyIdeas.cue: Why is whole genome sequencing useful now and in future?
keyIdeas.answer: It has become far faster and cheaper. Current uses include research into evolutionary relationships; future uses include personalised medicine (choosing drugs and doses based on a patient's genome).

keyIdeas.cue: Why doesn't the biological species concept suit asexual organisms and bacteria?
keyIdeas.answer: Asexual organisms don't interbreed at all, and bacteria swap genes between species by horizontal gene transfer, so 'can interbreed' doesn't define them.

keyIdeas.cue: Why is chromosome number a shared trait in a species?
keyIdeas.answer: Hybrids of parents with different chromosome numbers usually can't pair chromosomes in meiosis, so they are infertile (e.g. a mule from a horse with 64 and a donkey with 62).

keyIdeas.cue: How do you make a dichotomous key?
keyIdeas.answer: A series of numbered pairs of contrasting, observable statements (e.g. 'leaves needle-like / leaves broad'), each leading to another pair or a species name. Build one for local species.

keyIdeas.cue: How do eDNA and barcodes reveal biodiversity?
keyIdeas.answer: Environmental DNA (from water, soil, air) is sequenced; short standard gene regions (barcodes) are matched to a database to identify which species are present. It surveys habitats quickly without catching organisms.

keyTerms.def: Genus + species name, e.g. Homo sapiens.
Group that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
Image of chromosomes arranged in homologous pairs.
All the genetic information of an organism.
Transfer of genes between organisms other than by reproduction.
DNA collected from the environment, used to detect species.

workedExamples.title: Using a dichotomous key
workedExamples.prompt: 1a Wings present → 2; 1b No wings → spider. 2a Two wings → fly; 2b Four wings → 3. 3a Wings scaly → butterfly; 3b Wings clear → bee. Identify an animal with four clear wings.

misconceptions.wrong: Organisms that look alike are the same species.
misconceptions.right: Morphology can mislead; cryptic species look alike but don't interbreed.

misconceptions.wrong: Bigger genome means a more complex organism.
misconceptions.right: Genome size doesn't track complexity well.

misconceptions.wrong: The species name is written with a capital.
misconceptions.right: Only the genus has a capital: Homo sapiens.
